title: Halogenoalkanes: nucleophilic substitution; SN1 vs SN2
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for CCEA A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: OR09#t3 term and clue written for the game; OR09#t2 term and clue written for the game; OR09#t4 term and clue written for the game; OR09#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: OR09#N.3, OR10#N.4, OR09#N.6, OR10#N.6, OR09#N.9, OR10#N.13, OR09#N.12, OR10#N.14, OR09#N.14.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Curly arrow
items.clue: A two-barbed symbol that shows an electron pair moving.

items.label: Heterolytic fission
items.clue: A bond breaks with both bonding electrons going to one atom, so ions form.

items.label: Hydrolysis
items.clue: Another name for substitution of a halogenoalkane by OH⁻, giving an alcohol.

items.label: Nucleophile
items.clue: An electron-pair donor, attracted to a δ+ atom; OH⁻, CN⁻, NH₃ and H₂O are examples.

questions.stem: Which set contains only species that can act as nucleophiles?

options.text: OH⁻, H⁺, Br⁻
NH₃, H₂O, CN⁻
Cl⁻, NO₂⁺, H₂O
OH⁻, CN⁻, CH₄

questions.explanation: Each has a lone pair to donate: on N in NH₃, on O in H₂O, on C in CN⁻. A nucleophile need not be charged.

questions.stem: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₃CBr, reacts with aqueous hydroxide ions by the SN1 mechanism. Which describes the first step?

options.text: The C–Br bond breaks heterolytically, forming (CH₃)₃C⁺ and Br⁻.
OH⁻ attacks the C atom as the C–Br bond breaks, in a single step.
The C–Br bond breaks homolytically, giving radicals (CH₃)₃C• and Br•.
The C–Br bond breaks heterolytically, forming (CH₃)₃C⁻ and Br⁺ ions.

questions.explanation: The slow first step: Br takes the bonding pair (arrow from the C–Br bond to Br), giving a tertiary carbocation and Br⁻. OH⁻ attacks in the fast second step.

questions.stem: Hydroxide ions react with 1-chloropropane: CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + Cl⁻. Which describes the curly arrows correctly?

options.text: One arrow from a lone pair on the O of OH⁻ to the Cl atom; one from the C–Cl bond to the Cl atom.
One arrow from the C atom to the O of OH⁻; one from the Cl atom to the C–Cl bond.
One arrow from a lone pair on the O of OH⁻ to the C bonded to Cl; one from the C–Cl bond to Cl.
One arrow from a lone pair on the O of OH⁻ to the C atom; one from the C–Cl bond to the C atom.

questions.explanation: The O lone pair forms the new C–O bond, and the C–Cl bonding pair moves onto Cl, which leaves as Cl⁻.

questions.stem: A halogenoalkane, RX, is hydrolysed by OH⁻(aq). Illustrative initial-rate data: - Exp 1: [RX] 0.010, [OH⁻] 0.10 mol dm⁻³ → rate 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ - Exp 2: [RX] 0.020, [OH⁻] 0.10 mol dm⁻³ → rate 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ - Exp 3: [RX] 0.010, [OH⁻] 0.20 mol dm⁻³ → rate 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ Which rate equation and mechanism fit?

options.text: rate = k[RX][OH⁻]; SN2, with both species in one step
rate = k[OH⁻]; SN2, as OH⁻ is the attacking species
rate = k[RX]; SN2, because this mechanism has two steps
rate = k[RX]; SN1, with RX alone in the slow step

questions.explanation: First order in RX (Exp 1→2), zero order in OH⁻ (Exp 1→3). Only RX is in the rate-determining step: C–X breaks to a carbocation. Likely tertiary.

questions.stem: 1-chlorobutane, 1-bromobutane and 1-iodobutane are each added to aqueous silver nitrate in ethanol at 50 °C. Which tube shows a precipitate first, and what colour is it?

options.text: 1-iodobutane; yellow
1-chlorobutane; white
1-iodobutane; cream
All three at once, as water attacks each carbon equally

questions.explanation: C–I (228 kJ mol⁻¹) is the weakest C–X bond, so I⁻ is released fastest. AgI is yellow.

questions.stem: Which statement about the mechanisms of nucleophilic substitution of halogenoalkanes is correct?

options.text: Secondary ones react by SN1 and SN2, as both paths are feasible.
Primary ones react by SN1, as their carbocations are most stable.
Tertiary ones react by SN1, which takes place in one step.
Primary ones react via a stable intermediate with five bonds to C.

questions.explanation: Primary react by SN2 and tertiary by SN1. A secondary carbocation is of intermediate stability and backside attack only partly hindered, so both occur.

questions.stem: Bromoethane is heated with excess ammonia in ethanol: CH₃CH₂Br + 2NH₃ → CH₃CH₂NH₂ + NH₄Br. What does the second NH₃ molecule do?

options.text: It attacks the δ+ carbon again, so two NH₃ add to each carbon.
It supplies the two H atoms of the NH₂ group in the amine.
It reacts directly with Br⁻ to make NH₄Br.
It acts as a base, removing H⁺ from the CH₃CH₂NH₃⁺ ion.

questions.explanation: The first NH₃ is the nucleophile, giving CH₃CH₂NH₃⁺. The second uses its lone pair to take H⁺, giving the amine and NH₄⁺.

questions.stem: Two isomers of C₅H₁₁Cl are each hydrolysed by OH⁻(aq). Doubling [OH⁻] doubles the rate for 1-chloropentane, but leaves the rate unchanged for 2-chloro-2-methylbutane. Which statement is correct?

options.text: 1-chloropentane: SN1 via a carbocation · 2-chloro-2-methylbutane: SN2 in one step
1-chloropentane: SN2 in two steps · 2-chloro-2-methylbutane: SN1 in one step
1-chloropentane: SN2 in one step · 2-chloro-2-methylbutane: SN1 via a carbocation
1-chloropentane: SN2 via an intermediate · 2-chloro-2-methylbutane: SN1 via a carbocation

questions.explanation: Primary: OH⁻ in the one step, rate = k[RCl][OH⁻]. Tertiary: slow C–Cl break to a stable tertiary carbocation, rate = k[RCl].

questions.stem: Iodoethane, CH₃CH₂I, is warmed with aqueous sodium hydroxide, and ethanol forms. Which statement about the electron pairs is correct?

options.text: One electron from O and one from C form the C–O bond; I leaves as an atom, I•.
A lone pair on O forms the C–O bond; the C–I pair leaves with I, as I⁻.
The C–I pair moves across to O to become the C–O bond; I leaves as I⁺.
A lone pair on O attacks the δ− iodine atom, and the C–I pair moves onto carbon.

questions.explanation: OH⁻ is the nucleophile: its lone pair goes to the δ+ carbon. The C–I bond breaks heterolytically, and I⁻ leaves.
